rationale: A wins because it finds the buried economics, not just the announcement wrapper. Its "Perplexity is now paid twice on the same answer — and the publisher gets a slice of one payment" is risky, but it names the kill condition and the proof that would make or break the story. B's "tests how AI search actually makes money" is true enough and soft enough to be a conference-panel prompt. B is usable; A is the one a founder could take into a real editorial conversation.
gaps_in_A: "Perplexity starts paying publishers it was being sued over" overclaims the source facts. The update says criticism and legal threats, not filed lawsuits.
"Perplexity is now paid twice on the same answer" is the sharpest angle, but the headline asserts the thing the proof section admits still needs confirmation.
"A multi-billion-dollar valuation now has two revenue lines to defend it" is rightly labeled thin; without revenue figures or an investor on record, it is a VC-flavored question, not yet a story.
gaps_in_B: "subscription revenue alone hasn't proven out for AI answer engines" is not in the update. That is outside market color smuggled in as fact.

"The publishers threatening Perplexity with lawsuits are the same ones it's now offering to pay" overstates both the legal posture and the identity match. Legal threats are not necessarily lawsuits, and no participating publisher is named.

"Proof it needs: any disclosed adoption, transaction-volume, or attach-rate data...; company comment on strategy" is too soft for the lead monetization angle. A company comment is not proof; it is usually the fog machine.

B misses the sharper money-pool question. It says "two new revenue mechanisms launched together" but never asks whether a publisher whose review drives a purchase shares in the referral fee or only the ad revenue.
